title: Pray for the living and the dead
word: Pray for the living and the dead
hook: Francis also added care for our common home as a work of mercy (2016)
tomorrow: what does your mind grab first when you wake up?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: bear it. No revenge, and still the truth. Today, the last of the works of mercy, and a question families argue over.

Some phones still hold the contact of someone who died. Nobody can bring themselves to delete it. Families keep talking to their dead in other ways too, and at one graveside two cousins disagree. One says: pray for Grandpa. The other says: Grandpa was a saint. Pray to him. Both are Catholic. Both are sure. And both, it turns out, have the tradition on their side.
screen: `A CONTACT NOBODY DELETES.` → `PRAY FOR GRANDPA?` → `OR PRAY TO HIM?`

segments.voice: View one: pray for them. The second book of Maccabees, in Catholic Bibles, tells of Judas Maccabeus sending an offering to Jerusalem for soldiers who had died, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins." Catholics pray this way at funerals and on All Souls' Day, trusting that the dead still being made ready for God can be helped. At graves people still say, eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord. Its best case is humility: only God knows a soul, so love keeps praying. View two: ask them to pray for us. The Church teaches the communion of saints, the living and the dead in Christ as one family. Its best case: love doesn't end at death, and a grandmother who prayed for you every day may still be doing it. The Catechism holds both in one sentence: our prayer for the dead can help them, and can make their prayer for us effective. The one line the Church draws: public honor as a saint is kept for those it has declared saints. And the living? Paul asks for prayers for everyone, rulers included. Pope Francis also proposed care for our common home, the earth, as a work of mercy. Two cousins, one family, one line: pray for them.
screen: `A HOLY AND WHOLESOME THOUGHT.` · `ONE FAMILY, LIVING AND DEAD.` · `BOTH, IN ONE SENTENCE.` · `AND OUR COMMON HOME.` · then, large: `PRAY FOR THEM.`

segments.voice: Say two names out loud, softly: one living person you love, and one who has died. Add more if they come, living and dead side by side, the way Catholics name them at Mass. If you pray, you can pray for each one as you say the name; if not, let saying them keep them close.
Pray for the living and the dead. Hold them all before God, on both sides of death.
screen: `PRAY FOR THE LIVING AND THE DEAD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: pray for them. For the dead, with the dead, and for everyone still here. Good night.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for the living and the dead at every Mass, offer Masses for those who have died, keep All Souls' Day in November, and ask the saints and their own faithful dead to pray for them.

chat.meaning: The Church prays for the dead and believes they pray for us; the Catechism ties the two together in one sentence.
